title: Leg 59 — Elk Mountain and Vedauwoo to Cheyenne
subtitle: Elk Mountain, Laramie Basin, Vedauwoo and Cheyenne
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Rawlins and heading east across southern Wyoming toward Elk Mountain, then on through the Laramie Basin and the granite country around Vedauwoo before descending toward Cheyenne. The route crosses one of America's great transportation corridors, where stage roads, the Union Pacific, the Lincoln Highway and Interstate 80 repeatedly followed or reinvented the same passage through the mountains. Elk Mountain will sit off the right side of our eastbound pass, and the granite knobs of Vedauwoo will come close on the left later in the flight. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving Rawlins
blocks.text: We are leaving Rawlins behind and settling into the broad high country of southern Wyoming. Out here, distance can be deceptive: the land looks almost level from altitude, but low rims, shallow basins and long folds quietly control where roads, railroads and settlements can go.

blocks.title: High desert and open range
blocks.text: This is sagebrush country, dry and exposed, with ranching and transportation corridors often far more obvious than towns. The openness is useful on a flight like this because the big landforms ahead stand out early, especially Elk Mountain, which rises abruptly from the surrounding plains.

blocks.title: A transportation corridor reused again and again
blocks.text: Across southern Wyoming, generations of travelers kept rediscovering roughly the same east-west corridor. Stage routes came first, then the Union Pacific railroad, then the Lincoln Highway, U.S. 30 and eventually Interstate 80. Each generation changed the technology, but the mountains kept controlling the choices.

blocks.title: Elk Mountain ahead-right
blocks.text: Elk Mountain should now be the dominant massif ahead and to the right. Its summit reaches about eleven thousand one hundred fifty-six feet, so at our planned altitude we are only modestly higher than the top even though our route stays north of it.

blocks.title: A stage stop beneath Elk Mountain
blocks.text: The little community of Elk Mountain grew beside a crossing of the Medicine Bow River used by the Overland Trail. Stagecoach operator Ben Holladay shifted his route this way in the 1860s, and the site later became home to the Elk Mountain Hotel. The surviving hotel dates from the early twentieth century, but the location had already been serving travelers for decades.

blocks.title: Louis Armstrong in tiny Elk Mountain
blocks.text: Elk Mountain also had an unexpectedly glamorous chapter. In the 1940s and 1950s, the Garden Spot Pavilion beside the hotel drew large crowds to a dance floor built on springs. Big-name performers played there, including country star Hank Thompson and Louis Armstrong. It is a remarkable music story for a place that today feels so small and remote.

blocks.title: The Overland Trail east of Elk Mountain
blocks.text: As Elk Mountain begins to slip behind, we are near country crossed by the Overland Trail. Through this part of Wyoming the trail passed north of Elk Mountain along Rattlesnake Creek, connecting stage stops and river crossings on a route that linked the plains with the interior West.

blocks.title: Why the first highway avoided Elk Mountain
blocks.text: When the Lincoln Highway was laid out for automobiles, its route did not simply follow today's Interstate 80. West of Laramie it stayed closer to the Union Pacific through Rock River and Medicine Bow. Elk Mountain residents wanted the highway farther south, but that route came with weather concerns and, remarkably, would have required motorists to open and close thirty-two private-land gates.

blocks.title: Eisenhower crossed this country at five miles an hour
blocks.text: In 1919 a transcontinental Army convoy crossed Wyoming on the Lincoln Highway with a young Dwight Eisenhower along for the ride. The convoy averaged only about five miles an hour across the country, fighting dust, breakdowns, sand and primitive bridges. Eisenhower later wrote that the experience helped convince him of the need for far better national highways.

blocks.title: Interstate 80 chose the harder shortcut
blocks.text: Decades later, engineers faced the old route question again. Interstate 80 was ultimately pushed along the more direct line nearer Elk Mountain instead of following U.S. 30 north through Medicine Bow. Wyoming officials warned about winter weather, and only four days after the Laramie-to-Walcott section opened in 1970, an early snowstorm created exactly the kind of trouble they had feared.

blocks.title: Ancient rock south of the route
blocks.text: Off to the right, the Medicine Bow Mountains expose a very old Rocky Mountain core. U.S. Geological Survey mapping identifies Precambrian rocks here ranging back well over a billion years. They belong to a landscape far older than the younger sedimentary basins spread across much of southern Wyoming.

blocks.title: Opening into the Laramie Basin
blocks.text: The terrain ahead is opening into the Laramie Basin, a broad high plain between mountain ranges. This flatter country gave the railroad and later highways a workable approach toward the difficult crossing of the Laramie Range farther east.

blocks.title: Laramie off the left side
blocks.text: Laramie lies off to the left as we cross the basin. The town sprang up with the Union Pacific in 1868 and briefly had the wild atmosphere of an end-of-track railroad camp before settling into a permanent community tied to railroading, ranching and eventually the University of Wyoming.

blocks.title: Louisa Swain and a Wyoming first
blocks.text: Laramie became internationally important in the story of women's voting rights. Wyoming Territory granted women equal voting rights in 1869, and on September sixth, 1870, seventy-year-old Louisa Swain of Laramie cast the first documented woman's vote in a Wyoming general election. She was one of ninety-three women who voted in Laramie that day.

blocks.title: Toward the Laramie Range
blocks.text: The basin is beginning to tighten as we approach the Laramie Range. This crossing has always been the difficult part of the corridor: railroad engineers, motorists and highway builders all had to solve the same basic problem of gaining elevation without making the route too steep or too exposed.

blocks.title: Sherman Hill
blocks.text: We are now crossing the high Sherman Hill country between Laramie and Cheyenne. The original Union Pacific climbed to more than eight thousand feet here, making this one of the defining engineering obstacles on the transcontinental railroad.

blocks.title: The Ames Monument
blocks.text: Near the old railroad summit stands one of Wyoming's strangest monuments: a sixty-foot granite pyramid honoring Union Pacific financiers Oakes and Oliver Ames. Completed in 1882, it once stood beside the tracks at the railroad's highest point. The railroad was rerouted a few miles away in 1901, leaving the massive monument commemorating a line that no longer passes it.

blocks.title: A monument built after scandal
blocks.text: The monument was also an attempt to rehabilitate a damaged reputation. Oakes Ames became entangled in the Crédit Mobilier railroad-financing scandal and was censured by Congress. Yet the Union Pacific later honored the brothers with this expensive stone pyramid, designed by architect Henry Hobson Richardson with sculpted portraits by Augustus Saint-Gaudens.

blocks.title: Vedauwoo close on the left
blocks.text: Vedauwoo should be close on the left now, a jumble of rounded granite knobs and stacked-looking formations rising from Pole Mountain. The name is commonly traced to the Arapaho word bito'o'wu, often translated as earth-born, which fits the way these rocks seem to emerge directly from the landscape.

blocks.title: Ancient granite and modern climbing
blocks.text: Vedauwoo's formations are carved from roughly one-point-four-billion-year-old Sherman Granite. Weathering opened cracks and rounded the blocks into the shapes below. After World War Two, veterans of the Tenth Mountain Division helped establish modern climbing here, and Vedauwoo eventually became famous for demanding crack routes that attract climbers from far beyond Wyoming.

blocks.title: Leaving the granite high country
blocks.text: East of Vedauwoo the character of the flight changes again. The granite high country begins giving way toward the broad plains around Cheyenne. This is the same transition that made Cheyenne such an important junction: westbound traffic had mountains immediately ahead, while eastbound routes opened onto the Great Plains.

blocks.title: The railroad made Cheyenne possible
blocks.spokenLabel: the Union Pacific approach to Cheyenne
blocks.text: The Union Pacific reached Cheyenne in November 1867, before tackling the climb over the Laramie Range. Because construction paused here for months, the temporary end-of-track settlement had more time than most railroad camps to turn itself into a real town. The railroad also chose Cheyenne for major shops and a depot, giving it a reason to survive after the track crews moved on.

blocks.title: Cheyenne ahead
blocks.text: Cheyenne should now be becoming part of the view ahead. It grew so quickly after the railroad arrived that it earned the nickname Magic City of the Plains. What began as Crow Creek Crossing in 1867 became the territorial capital and then the capital of Wyoming.

blocks.title: Frontier Days
blocks.text: Cheyenne's best-known tradition began in 1897. The first Frontier Day was conceived as a western celebration with bronc riding, horse races, stagecoaches and other events, and thousands of visitors arrived by rail. It grew into Cheyenne Frontier Days, turning the city's cattle and railroad heritage into one of its defining public traditions.

blocks.title: Cheyenne's aviation chapter
blocks.text: The airport ahead has its own unusually rich history. Cheyenne became a major transcontinental aviation stop in the 1930s. During World War Two, United Airlines operated a large modification center here that upgraded thousands of military bombers, and after the war United trained more than six thousand stewardesses in Cheyenne before moving the school to Chicago in 1961.

blocks.title: Cheyenne Regional Airport
blocks.text: Cheyenne Regional Airport is just ahead now. This is a fitting place to finish a leg built around transportation history: stage roads, railroad grades, early highways, interstates and aviation all overlap in this corner of Wyoming.
